title: Lewis Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Lewis wells have a 125-foot median depth and typical finished-well costs of $12,200-$21,400. Review local yield and permitting data.
h1: What Lewis, Colorado Well Records Show
intro_html:
For rural property around Lewis, the available well records point to a generally moderate drilling depth, but the local spread is wide. The median reported depth is 125 feet, while the middle half runs from 70 to 220 feet. The deepest record reaches 885 feet.

Yield records are limited, with only 12 wells reporting a pump yield. Among those, the median is 4.5 gallons per minute. Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, so nearby well results are useful but cannot guarantee what a new hole will produce on a particular lot.

sections.heading: Lewis well depths vary well beyond the median
sections.html:
The 125-foot median is a reasonable starting point for a preliminary drilling conversation around Lewis, but it is not a promise of finished depth. Half of the wells with reported depths fall between 70 and 220 feet. Another 14% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 8% exceed 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 885 feet.

Depth records also show that 37% are under 100 feet and 41% fall between 100 and 300 feet. For a driller's bid, that means a median-depth estimate may be useful for budgeting, while the high-end records justify asking about a deeper-hole rate, casing, grout, and what happens if the first target does not produce.

sections.heading: What a Lewis well may produce
sections.html:
The reported yield picture is stronger than the depth range, but the sample is small: only 12 permits report a pump yield. The median reported yield is 4.5 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 3.8 to 8.1 gallons per minute. Half of the reported wells fall in the 1-to-5-gallon-per-minute range, while 42% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute.

No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute, and 8% are above 15 gallons per minute. For a buyer, a 4.5-gallon-per-minute result can support ordinary household planning with appropriate storage, but it does not establish irrigation capacity. Confirm the permitted use and obtain a pump test before relying on a particular parcel.

sections.heading: Lewis water levels cannot yet show a trend
sections.html:
No well in the available Lewis records reports a static water level. That leaves no water-level-by-decade series to show whether the local water table is stable, rising, or dropping. A driller may encounter water while drilling, but that observation is not the same as a measured static level after the well has recovered.

Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer: 105 wells use that description. Two name the Dakota aquifer and one names the Entrada. Fractured rock can produce uneven results over short distances, so ask for the neighboring well logs, construction details, tested yield, and static water level rather than assuming every lot shares the same groundwater conditions.

sections.heading: Lewis permit history and local drillers
sections.html:
The permit record stretches from the 1950s through a newest permit year of 2025. Activity was highest in the 2000s, with 25 permits issued in that decade. The 1980s account for 12, the 1970s for 6, and the 1990s for 4. Earlier decades show 1 permit in the 1950s and 1 in the 1960s; the 2010s show 2, followed by 1 in the 2020s.

Among the drillers appearing most often, Mcpherson Drilling Co. (Mcpherson, Billy G.) appears on 16 records, Ancell Drilling Service (Ancell, Lee) on 6, and Kenyon Drilling/Kenyon Motor (Kenyon, W K) on 5. These records describe past work, not current availability, so verify licensing, scheduling, and scope directly.

sections.heading: Lewis drilling cost at local depths
sections.html:
The cost model for Lewis assumes mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground and a drilling rate of $50 to $75 per foot. At the 125-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $6,200 to $9,400. That is only the hole, not a complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $12,200 to $21,400 at that median depth. A deeper-than-typical hole can move the total higher, especially when casing, grout, difficult access, or additional trenching is involved. Ask for a written allowance that separates drilling from pump equipment and site work.

sections.heading: Lewis water, septic, and lot risks to check
sections.html:
There are 9 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles of Lewis. That does not establish contamination on a particular property, but it makes water testing an important part of due diligence. Test the existing well, review construction and treatment history, and confirm the laboratory and sampling method before closing.

The records show 51% domestic or household permits, 14% stock, 1% irrigation, and 7% monitoring. A well's permitted use matters if your plan includes more than ordinary household use. Exempt household-use wells also have a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit. Check DWR records and current water-right requirements, including augmentation needs in an over-appropriated basin. Before building, confirm septic setbacks, usable drainfield area, access for a rig, electrical routing, and whether the lot can accommodate the house, well, and septic system together.

sections.heading: Buying or building near Lewis
sections.html:
Start by collecting the DWR permit and construction records for the property and nearby wells. Compare depth, aquifer description, casing and grout, pump test results, and static water level where those details exist. The 70-to-220-foot middle range is useful for comparing neighboring bids, but the 885-foot deepest record shows why a fixed shallow estimate can be risky.

For vacant land, make the purchase agreement address well location, drilling access, water testing, and what happens if the hole is dry or has inadequate yield. Nearby Dolores, Cortez, and Towaoc may help with broader contractor and service planning, but the well evidence should stay focused on the immediate area around Lewis. Have a Colorado water-rights professional review the intended use before construction begins.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Lewis, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Lewis is 125 feet, and the middle half ranges from 70 to 220 feet. About 37% are under 100 feet and 41% are between 100 and 300 feet. Depth can vary sharply, though: the deepest record is 885 feet, so a nearby shallow well does not guarantee a shallow new hole.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Lewis, Colorado?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $75 per foot in mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 125-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $6,200 to $9,400. A finished well including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $12,200 to $21,400. Deeper drilling or difficult access can increase the bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Lewis?
faq.a: Only 12 Lewis-area records report a pump yield. The median reported yield is 4.5 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 3.8 to 8.1 gallons per minute. Half report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, and 42% report 5 to 15. These figures are planning guidance, not a guarantee for a new well.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Lewis, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from the permit record alone. There are 9 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, so test an existing or new well through a qualified laboratory. Review treatment history and construction records as well. A nearby permit or acceptable yield does not prove that water quality on your property is safe.

faq.q: Are Lewis wells in a declining water table?
faq.a: The available records cannot establish a declining water table because 0 wells report a static water level. Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, which can vary substantially between nearby locations. Before buying, request neighboring well logs and measured static levels where available, and have the proposed use reviewed for applicable Colorado water-right requirements.
